tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

schema.name: Bash
schema.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

<cell id="cell-2"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type># Gradient Checkpointing Demo (Network-in-Network trained on CIFAR-10)</cell id="cell-2">
<cell id="cell-3"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>


Why do we care about gradient checkpointing? It can lower the memory requirement of deep neural networks quite substantially, allowing us to work with larger architectures and memory limitations of conventional GPUs. However, there is no free lunch here: as a trade-off for the lower-memory requirements, additional computations are carried out which can prolong the training time. However, when GPU-memory is a limiting factor that we cannot even circumvent by lowering the batch sizes, then gradient checkpointing is a great and easy option for making things work!

Below is a brief summary of how gradient checkpointing works. For more details, please see the excellent explanations in [1] and [2].

## Vanilla Backpropagation

In vanilla backpropagation (the standard version of backpropagation), the required memory grows linearly with the number of layers *n* in the neural network. This is because all nodes from the forward pass are being kept in memory (until all their dependent child nodes are processed).

![](figures/gradient-checkpointing-1.png)

## Low-memory Backpropagation

In the low-memory version of backpropagation, the forward pass is recomputed at each step, making it more memory-efficient than vanilla backpropagation, trading the memory for additional computations. In comparison, vanilla backpropagation processes *n* layers (nodes), the low-memory version processes $n^2$ nodes.

![](figures/gradient-checkpointing-2.png)

## Gradient Checkpointing

The gradient checkpointing method is a compromise between vanilla backpropagation and low-memory backpropagation, where nodes are recomputed more often than in vanilla backpropagation but not as often as in the low-memory version. In gradient checkpointing, we designate certain nodes as checkpoints so that they are not recomputed and serve as a basis for recomputing other nodes. The optimal choice is to designate every `\sqrt{n}`-th node as a checkpoint node. Consequently, the memory requirement increases by `\sqrt{n}` compared to the low-memory version of backpropagation.

As stated in [3], gradient checkpointing, we can implement models that are 4x to 10x larger than architectures that would usually fit into GPU memory.

![](figures/gradient-checkpointing-3.png)

## Gradient Checkpointing in PyTorch

PyTorch allows us to use gradient checkpointing very conveniently. In this notebook, we are only using the checkpointing for sequential models. However, it is also possible (and not much more complicated) to use checkpointing for non-sequential models. I recommend checking out the tutorial in [3] for more details.

A great performance benchmark and write-up is available at [4], showing the difference in memory consumption between a baseline ResNet-18 and one enhanced with gradient checkpointing.




References
-----------


[1] Saving memory using gradient-checkpointing: https://github.com/cybertronai/gradient-checkpointing

[2] Fitting larger networks into memory: https://medium.com/tensorflow/fitting-larger-networks-into-memory-583e3c758ff9

[3] Trading compute for memory in PyTorch models using Checkpointing: https://github.com/prigoyal/pytorch_memonger/blob/master/tutorial/Checkpointing_for_PyTorch_models.ipynb

[4] Deep Learning Memory Usage and Pytorch Optimization Tricks: https://www.sicara.ai/blog/2019-28-10-deep-learning-memory-usage-and-pytorch-optimization-tricks</cell id="cell-3">

<cell id="cell-30"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>The changes we have to make to the NiN code are highlighted below. Note that this example uses only 1 segment in `checkpoint_sequential`. Generally, a lower number of segments improves memory efficiency but making the computational performance worse since more values need to be recomputed. For this architecture, I found that `segments=1` represents a good trade-off, though.</cell id="cell-30">
<cell id="cell-31">##########################
### MODEL
##########################


###### NEW ####################################################
from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint_sequential
###############################################################


class NiN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_classes):
        super(NiN, self).__init__()
        self.num_classes = num_classes
        self.classifier = nn.Sequential(
                nn.Conv2d(3, 192, kernel_size=5, stride=1, padding=2),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 160, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(160,  96, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1),
                nn.Dropout(0.5),

                nn.Conv2d(96, 192, kernel_size=5, stride=1, padding=2),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1),
                nn.Dropout(0.5),

                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192,  10, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size=8, stride=1, padding=0),
                )
        
        ###### NEW ####################################################
        self.classifier_modules = [module for k, module in self.classifier._modules.items()]
        ###############################################################

    def forward(self, x):
        
        ###### NEW ####################################################
        x.requires_grad = True
        x = checkpoint_sequential(functions=self.classifier_modules, 
                                  segments=1, 
                                  input=x)
        ###############################################################
        
        x = x.view(x.size(0), self.num_classes)
        #probas = torch.softmax(x, dim=1)
        return x</cell id="cell-31">

<cell id="cell-2"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type># Gradient Checkpointing Demo (Network-in-Network trained on CIFAR-10)</cell id="cell-2">
<cell id="cell-3"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>


Why do we care about gradient checkpointing? It can lower the memory requirement of deep neural networks quite substantially, allowing us to work with larger architectures and memory limitations of conventional GPUs. However, there is no free lunch here: as a trade-off for the lower-memory requirements, additional computations are carried out which can prolong the training time. However, when GPU-memory is a limiting factor that we cannot even circumvent by lowering the batch sizes, then gradient checkpointing is a great and easy option for making things work!

Below is a brief summary of how gradient checkpointing works. For more details, please see the excellent explanations in [1] and [2].

## Vanilla Backpropagation

In vanilla backpropagation (the standard version of backpropagation), the required memory grows linearly with the number of layers *n* in the neural network. This is because all nodes from the forward pass are being kept in memory (until all their dependent child nodes are processed).

![](figures/gradient-checkpointing-1.png)

## Low-memory Backpropagation

In the low-memory version of backpropagation, the forward pass is recomputed at each step, making it more memory-efficient than vanilla backpropagation, trading the memory for additional computations. In comparison, vanilla backpropagation processes *n* layers (nodes), the low-memory version processes $n^2$ nodes.

![](figures/gradient-checkpointing-2.png)

## Gradient Checkpointing

The gradient checkpointing method is a compromise between vanilla backpropagation and low-memory backpropagation, where nodes are recomputed more often than in vanilla backpropagation but not as often as in the low-memory version. In gradient checkpointing, we designate certain nodes as checkpoints so that they are not recomputed and serve as a basis for recomputing other nodes. The optimal choice is to designate every `\sqrt{n}`-th node as a checkpoint node. Consequently, the memory requirement increases by `\sqrt{n}` compared to the low-memory version of backpropagation.

As stated in [3], gradient checkpointing, we can implement models that are 4x to 10x larger than architectures that would usually fit into GPU memory.

![](figures/gradient-checkpointing-3.png)

## Gradient Checkpointing in PyTorch

PyTorch allows us to use gradient checkpointing very conveniently. In this notebook, we are only using the checkpointing for sequential models. However, it is also possible (and not much more complicated) to use checkpointing for non-sequential models. I recommend checking out the tutorial in [3] for more details.

A great performance benchmark and write-up is available at [4], showing the difference in memory consumption between a baseline ResNet-18 and one enhanced with gradient checkpointing.




References
-----------


[1] Saving memory using gradient-checkpointing: https://github.com/cybertronai/gradient-checkpointing

[2] Fitting larger networks into memory: https://medium.com/tensorflow/fitting-larger-networks-into-memory-583e3c758ff9

[3] Trading compute for memory in PyTorch models using Checkpointing: https://github.com/prigoyal/pytorch_memonger/blob/master/tutorial/Checkpointing_for_PyTorch_models.ipynb

[4] Deep Learning Memory Usage and Pytorch Optimization Tricks: https://www.sicara.ai/blog/2019-28-10-deep-learning-memory-usage-and-pytorch-optimization-tricks</cell id="cell-3">

<cell id="cell-30"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>The changes we have to make to the NiN code are highlighted below. Note that this example uses only 1 segment in `checkpoint_sequential`. ### MODEL
##########################


###### NEW ####################################################
from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint_sequential
###############################################################


class NiN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_classes):
        super(NiN, self).__init__()
        self.num_classes = num_classes
        self.classifier = nn.Sequential(
                nn.Conv2d(3, 192, kernel_size=5, stride=1, padding=2),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 160, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(160,  96, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1),
                nn.Dropout(0.5),

                nn.Conv2d(96, 192, kernel_size=5, stride=1, padding=2),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1),
                nn.Dropout(0.5),

                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192,  10, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size=8, stride=1, padding=0),
                )
        
        ###### NEW ####################################################
        self.classifier_modules = [module for k, module in self.classifier._modules.items()]
        ###############################################################

    def forward(self, x):
        
        ###### NEW ####################################################
        x.requires_grad = True
        x = checkpoint_sequential(functions=self.classifier_modules, 
                                  segments=1, 
                                  input=x)
        ###############################################################
        
        x = x.view(x.size(0), self.num_classes)
        #probas = torch.softmax(x, dim=1)
        return x</cell id="cell-31">

<cell id="cell-3"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>


Why do we care about gradient checkpointing? It can lower the memory requirement of deep neural networks quite substantially, allowing us to work with larger architectures and memory limitations of conventional GPUs. However, there is no free lunch here: as a trade-off for the lower-memory requirements, additional computations are carried out which can prolong the training time. However, when GPU-memory is a limiting factor that we cannot even circumvent by lowering the batch sizes, then gradient checkpointing is a great and easy option for making things work!

Below is a brief summary of how gradient checkpointing works. For more details, please see the excellent explanations in [1] and [2].

## Vanilla Backpropagation

In vanilla backpropagation (the standard version of backpropagation), the required memory grows linearly with the number of layers *n* in the neural network. This is because all nodes from the forward pass are being kept in memory (until all their dependent child nodes are processed).

![](figures/gradient-checkpointing-1.png)

## Low-memory Backpropagation

In the low-memory version of backpropagation, the forward pass is recomputed at each step, making it more memory-efficient than vanilla backpropagation, trading the memory for additional computations. In comparison, vanilla backpropagation processes *n* layers (nodes), the low-memory version processes $n^2$ nodes.

![](figures/gradient-checkpointing-2.png)

## Gradient Checkpointing

The gradient checkpointing method is a compromise between vanilla backpropagation and low-memory backpropagation, where nodes are recomputed more often than in vanilla backpropagation but not as often as in the low-memory version. In gradient checkpointing, we designate certain nodes as checkpoints so that they are not recomputed and serve as a basis for recomputing other nodes. The optimal choice is to designate every `\sqrt{n}`-th node as a checkpoint node. Consequently, the memory requirement increases by `\sqrt{n}` compared to the low-memory version of backpropagation.

As stated in [3], gradient checkpointing, we can implement models that are 4x to 10x larger than architectures that would usually fit into GPU memory.

![](figures/gradient-checkpointing-3.png)

## Gradient Checkpointing in PyTorch

PyTorch allows us to use gradient checkpointing very conveniently. In this notebook, we are only using the checkpointing for sequential models. However, it is also possible (and not much more complicated) to use checkpointing for non-sequential models. I recommend checking out the tutorial in [3] for more details.

A great performance benchmark and write-up is available at [4], showing the difference in memory consumption between a baseline ResNet-18 and one enhanced with gradient checkpointing.




References
-----------


[1] Saving memory using gradient-checkpointing: https://github.com/cybertronai/gradient-checkpointing

[2] Fitting larger networks into memory: https://medium.com/tensorflow/fitting-larger-networks-into-memory-583e3c758ff9

[3] Trading compute for memory in PyTorch models using Checkpointing: https://github.com/prigoyal/pytorch_memonger/blob/master/tutorial/Checkpointing_for_PyTorch_models.ipynb

[4] Deep Learning Memory Usage and Pytorch Optimization Tricks: https://www.sicara.ai/blog/2019-28-10-deep-learning-memory-usage-and-pytorch-optimization-tricks</cell id="cell-3">

                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1),
                nn.Dropout(0.5),

                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192,  10, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size=8, stride=1, padding=0),
                )

        x = checkpoint_sequential(functions=self.classifier_modules, 
                                  segments=1, 
                                  input=x)

<cell id="cell-2"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type># Gradient Checkpointing Demo (Network-in-Network trained on CIFAR-10)</cell id="cell-2">
<cell id="cell-3"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>


Why do we care about gradient checkpointing? It can lower the memory requirement of deep neural networks quite substantially, allowing us to work with larger architectures and memory limitations of conventional GPUs. However, there is no free lunch here: as a trade-off for the lower-memory requirements, additional computations are carried out which can prolong the training time. However, when GPU-memory is a limiting factor that we cannot even circumvent by lowering the batch sizes, then gradient checkpointing is a great and easy option for making things work!

Below is a brief summary of how gradient checkpointing works. For more details, please see the excellent explanations in [1] and [2].

## Vanilla Backpropagation

In vanilla backpropagation (the standard version of backpropagation), the required memory grows linearly with the number of layers *n* in the neural network. This is because all nodes from the forward pass are being kept in memory (until all their dependent child nodes are processed).

![](figures/gradient-checkpointing-1.png)

## Low-memory Backpropagation

In the low-memory version of backpropagation, the forward pass is recomputed at each step, making it more memory-efficient than vanilla backpropagation, trading the memory for additional computations. In comparison, vanilla backpropagation processes *n* layers (nodes), the low-memory version processes $n^2$ nodes.

![](figures/gradient-checkpointing-2.png)

## Gradient Checkpointing

The gradient checkpointing method is a compromise between vanilla backpropagation and low-memory backpropagation, where nodes are recomputed more often than in vanilla backpropagation but not as often as in the low-memory version. In gradient checkpointing, we designate certain nodes as checkpoints so that they are not recomputed and serve as a basis for recomputing other nodes. The optimal choice is to designate every `\sqrt{n}`-th node as a checkpoint node. Consequently, the memory requirement increases by `\sqrt{n}` compared to the low-memory version of backpropagation.

As stated in [3], gradient checkpointing, we can implement models that are 4x to 10x larger than architectures that would usually fit into GPU memory.

![](figures/gradient-checkpointing-3.png)

## Gradient Checkpointing in PyTorch

PyTorch allows us to use gradient checkpointing very conveniently. In this notebook, we are only using the checkpointing for sequential models. However, it is also possible (and not much more complicated) to use checkpointing for non-sequential models. I recommend checking out the tutorial in [3] for more details.

A great performance benchmark and write-up is available at [4], showing the difference in memory consumption between a baseline ResNet-18 and one enhanced with gradient checkpointing.




References
-----------


[1] Saving memory using gradient-checkpointing: https://github.com/cybertronai/gradient-checkpointing

[2] Fitting larger networks into memory: https://medium.com/tensorflow/fitting-larger-networks-into-memory-583e3c758ff9

[3] Trading compute for memory in PyTorch models using Checkpointing: https://github.com/prigoyal/pytorch_memonger/blob/master/tutorial/Checkpointing_for_PyTorch_models.ipynb

[4] Deep Learning Memory Usage and Pytorch Optimization Tricks: https://www.sicara.ai/blog/2019-28-10-deep-learning-memory-usage-and-pytorch-optimization-tricks</cell id="cell-3">

# Gradient Checkpointing Demo (Network-in-Network trained on CIFAR-10)

Why do we care about gradient checkpointing? It can lower the memory requirement of deep neural networks quite substantially, allowing us to work with larger architectures and memory limitations of conventional GPUs. However, there is no free lunch here: as a trade-off for the lower-memory requirements, additional computations are carried out which can prolong the training time. However, when GPU-memory is a limiting factor that we cannot even circumvent by lowering the batch sizes, then gradient checkpointing is a great and easy option for making things work!

Below is a brief summary of how gradient checkpointing works. For more details, please see the excellent explanations in [1] and [2].

## Vanilla Backpropagation

In vanilla backpropagation (the standard version of backpropagation), the required memory grows linearly with the number of layers *n* in the neural network. This is because all nodes from the forward pass are being kept in memory (until all their dependent child nodes are processed).

![](figures/gradient-checkpointing-1.png)

## Low-memory Backpropagation

In the low-memory version of backpropagation, the forward pass is recomputed at each step, making it more memory-efficient than vanilla backpropagation, trading the memory for additional computations. In comparison, vanilla backpropagation processes *n* layers (nodes), the low-memory version processes $n^2$ nodes.

![](figures/gradient-checkpointing-2.png)

## Gradient Checkpointing

The gradient checkpointing method is a compromise between vanilla backpropagation and low-memory backpropagation, where nodes are recomputed more often than in vanilla backpropagation but not as often as in the low-memory version. In gradient checkpointing, we designate certain nodes as checkpoints so that they are not recomputed and serve as a basis for recomputing other nodes. The optimal choice is to designate every `\sqrt{n}`-th node as a checkpoint node. Consequently, the memory requirement increases by `\sqrt{n}` compared to the low-memory version of backpropagation.

As stated in [3], gradient checkpointing, we can implement models that are 4x to 10x larger than architectures that would usually fit into GPU memory.

![](figures/gradient-checkpointing-3.png)

## Gradient Checkpointing in PyTorch

PyTorch allows us to use gradient checkpointing very conveniently. In this notebook, we are only using the checkpointing for sequential models. However, it is also possible (and not much more complicated) to use checkpointing for non-sequential models. I recommend checking out the tutorial in [3] for more details.

A great performance benchmark and write-up is available at [4], showing the difference in memory consumption between a baseline ResNet-18 and one enhanced with gradient checkpointing.




References
-----------


[1] Saving memory using gradient-checkpointing: https://github.com/cybertronai/gradient-checkpointing

[2] Fitting larger networks into memory: https://medium.com/tensorflow/fitting-larger-networks-into-memory-583e3c758ff9

[3] Trading compute for memory in PyTorch models using Checkpointing: https://github.com/prigoyal/pytorch_memonger/blob/master/tutorial/Checkpointing_for_PyTorch_models.ipynb

[4] Deep Learning Memory Usage and Pytorch Optimization Tricks: https://www.sicara.ai/blog/2019-28-10-deep-learning-memory-usage-and-pytorch-optimization-tricks
### Network Architecture

For this demo, I am using a simple Network-in-Network (NiN) architecture for the purpose of code readability. The gain from gradient checkpointing can be larger the deeper the architecture. 


The CNN architecture is based on
- Lin, Min, Qiang Chen, and Shuicheng Yan. "Network in network." arXiv preprint arXiv:1312.4400 (2013).

This is the basic NiN model without gradient checkpointing for reference.

##########################
### MODEL
##########################

class NiN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_classes):
        super(NiN, self).__init__()
        self.num_classes = num_classes
        self.classifier = nn.Sequential(
                nn.Conv2d(3, 192, kernel_size=5, stride=1, padding=2),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 160, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(160,  96, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1),
                nn.Dropout(0.5),

                nn.Conv2d(96, 192, kernel_size=5, stride=1, padding=2),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1),
                nn.Dropout(0.5),

                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192,  10, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size=8, stride=1, padding=0),

                )

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.classifier(x)
        logits = x.view(x.size(0), self.num_classes)
        #probas = torch.softmax(logits, dim=1)
        return logits

set_all_seeds(RANDOM_SEED)

model = NiN(NUM_CLASSES)
model.to(DEVICE)

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=LEARNING_RATE)
## Training

import tracemalloc


tracemalloc.start()
log_dict = train_classifier_simple_v1(num_epochs=2, model=model, 
                                      optimizer=optimizer, device=DEVICE, 
                                      train_loader=train_loader, valid_loader=valid_loader,
                                      logging_interval=50)

current, peak =  tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()
print(f"{current}, {peak}")
tracemalloc.stop()

### Delete model and free memory

model.cpu()
del model
# Part 2: Modified NiN with Gradient Checkpointing

The changes we have to make to the NiN code are highlighted below. Note that this example uses only 1 segment in `checkpoint_sequential`. Generally, a lower number of segments improves memory efficiency but making the computational performance worse since more values need to be recomputed. For this architecture, I found that `segments=1` represents a good trade-off, though.

##########################
### MODEL
##########################


###### NEW ####################################################
from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint_sequential
###############################################################


class NiN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_classes):
        super(NiN, self).__init__()
        self.num_classes = num_classes
        self.classifier = nn.Sequential(
                nn.Conv2d(3, 192, kernel_size=5, stride=1, padding=2),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 160, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(160,  96, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1),
                nn.Dropout(0.5),

                nn.Conv2d(96, 192, kernel_size=5, stride=1, padding=2),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1),
                nn.Dropout(0.5),

                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192,  10, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size=8, stride=1, padding=0),
                )
        
        ###### NEW ####################################################
        self.classifier_modules = [module for k, module in self.classifier._modules.items()]
        ###############################################################

    def forward(self, x):
        
        ###### NEW ####################################################
        x.requires_grad = True
        x = checkpoint_sequential(functions=self.classifier_modules, 
                                  segments=1, 
                                  input=x)
        ###############################################################
        
        x = x.view(x.size(0), self.num_classes)
        #probas = torch.softmax(x, dim=1)
        return x

set_all_seeds(RANDOM_SEED)

model = NiN(NUM_CLASSES)
model.to(DEVICE)

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=LEARNING_RATE)

tracemalloc.start()
log_dict = train_classifier_simple_v1(num_epochs=2, model=model, 
                                      optimizer=optimizer, device=DEVICE, 
                                      train_loader=train_loader, valid_loader=valid_loader,
                                      logging_interval=50)

current, peak =  tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()
print(f"{current}, {peak}")
tracemalloc.stop()
# Conclusion
We can see that the gradient checkpointing improves peak memory efficiency by approximately 22% while the computational performance (runtime) becomes only 14% worse.

<cell id="cell-2"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type># Gradient Checkpointing Demo (Network-in-Network trained on CIFAR-10)</cell id="cell-2">
<cell id="cell-3"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>


Why do we care about gradient checkpointing? It can lower the memory requirement of deep neural networks quite substantially, allowing us to work with larger architectures and memory limitations of conventional GPUs. However, there is no free lunch here: as a trade-off for the lower-memory requirements, additional computations are carried out which can prolong the training time. However, when GPU-memory is a limiting factor that we cannot even circumvent by lowering the batch sizes, then gradient checkpointing is a great and easy option for making things work!

Below is a brief summary of how gradient checkpointing works. For more details, please see the excellent explanations in [1] and [2].

## Vanilla Backpropagation

In vanilla backpropagation (the standard version of backpropagation), the required memory grows linearly with the number of layers *n* in the neural network. This is because all nodes from the forward pass are being kept in memory (until all their dependent child nodes are processed).

![](figures/gradient-checkpointing-1.png)

## Low-memory Backpropagation

In the low-memory version of backpropagation, the forward pass is recomputed at each step, making it more memory-efficient than vanilla backpropagation, trading the memory for additional computations. In comparison, vanilla backpropagation processes *n* layers (nodes), the low-memory version processes $n^2$ nodes.

![](figures/gradient-checkpointing-2.png)

## Gradient Checkpointing

The gradient checkpointing method is a compromise between vanilla backpropagation and low-memory backpropagation, where nodes are recomputed more often than in vanilla backpropagation but not as often as in the low-memory version. In gradient checkpointing, we designate certain nodes as checkpoints so that they are not recomputed and serve as a basis for recomputing other nodes. The optimal choice is to designate every `\sqrt{n}`-th node as a checkpoint node. Consequently, the memory requirement increases by `\sqrt{n}` compared to the low-memory version of backpropagation.

As stated in [3], gradient checkpointing, we can implement models that are 4x to 10x larger than architectures that would usually fit into GPU memory.

![](figures/gradient-checkpointing-3.png)

## Gradient Checkpointing in PyTorch

PyTorch allows us to use gradient checkpointing very conveniently. In this notebook, we are only using the checkpointing for sequential models. However, it is also possible (and not much more complicated) to use checkpointing for non-sequential models. I recommend checking out the tutorial in [3] for more details.

A great performance benchmark and write-up is available at [4], showing the difference in memory consumption between a baseline ResNet-18 and one enhanced with gradient checkpointing.




References
-----------


[1] Saving memory using gradient-checkpointing: https://github.com/cybertronai/gradient-checkpointing

[2] Fitting larger networks into memory: https://medium.com/tensorflow/fitting-larger-networks-into-memory-583e3c758ff9

[3] Trading compute for memory in PyTorch models using Checkpointing: https://github.com/prigoyal/pytorch_memonger/blob/master/tutorial/Checkpointing_for_PyTorch_models.ipynb

[4] Deep Learning Memory Usage and Pytorch Optimization Tricks: https://www.sicara.ai/blog/2019-28-10-deep-learning-memory-usage-and-pytorch-optimization-tricks</cell id="cell-3">

The optimal choice is to designate every `\sqrt{n}`-th node as a checkpoint node. Consequently, the memory requirement increases by `\sqrt{n}` compared to the low-memory version of backpropagation.

As stated in [3], gradient checkpointing, we can implement models that are 4x to 10x larger than architectures that would usually fit into GPU memory.

![](figures/gradient-checkpointing-3.png)

## Gradient Checkpointing in PyTorch

PyTorch allows us to use gradient checkpointing very conveniently. In this notebook, we are only using the checkpointing for sequential models. However, it is also possible (and not much more complicated) to use checkpointing for non-sequential models. I recommend checking out the tutorial in [3] for more details.

A great performance benchmark and write-up is available at [4], showing the difference in memory consumption between a baseline ResNet-18 and one enhanced with gradient checkpointing.




References
-----------


[1] Saving memory using gradient-checkpointing: https://github.com/cybertronai/gradient-checkpointing

[2] Fitting larger networks into memory: https://medium.com/tensorflow/fitting-larger-networks-into-memory-583e3c758ff9

[3] Trading compute for memory in PyTorch models using Checkpointing: https://github.com/prigoyal/pytorch_memonger/blob/master/tutorial/Checkpointing_for_PyTorch_models.ipynb

[4] Deep Learning Memory Usage and Pytorch Optimization Tricks: https://www.sicara.ai/blog/2019-28-10-deep-learning-memory-usage-and-pytorch-optimization-tricks</cell id="cell-3">

<cell id="cell-30"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>The changes we have to make to the NiN code are highlighted below. Note that this example uses only 1 segment in `checkpoint_sequential`. Generally, a lower number of segments improves memory efficiency but making the computational performance worse since more values need to be recomputed. For this architecture, I found that `segments=1` represents a good trade-off, though.</cell id="cell-30">
<cell id="cell-31">##########################
### MODEL
##########################


###### NEW ####################################################
from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint_sequential
###############################################################


class NiN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_classes):
        super(NiN, self).__init__()
        self.num_classes = num_classes
        self.classifier = nn.Sequential(
                nn.Conv2d(3, 192, kernel_size=5, stride=1, padding=2),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 160, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(160,  96, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1),
                nn.Dropout(0.5),

                nn.Conv2d(96, 192, kernel_size=5, stride=1, padding=2),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1),
                nn.Dropout(0.5),

                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192, 192, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.Conv2d(192,  10, kernel_size=1, stride=1, padding=0),
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size=8, stride=1, padding=0),
                )
        
        ###### NEW ####################################################
        self.classifier_modules = [module for k, module in self.classifier._modules.items()]
        ###############################################################

    def forward(self, x):
        
        ###### NEW ####################################################
        x.requires_grad = True
        x = checkpoint_sequential(functions=self.classifier_modules, 
                                  segments=1, 
                                  input=x)
        ###############################################################
        
        x = x.view(x.size(0), self.num_classes)
        #probas = torch.softmax(x, dim=1)
        return x</cell id="cell-31">

关键点：本讲义的核心教学内容：

1. **为什么训练吃显存**：前向传播中每个中间激活（用于反向传播）都要保存。显存占用 ≈ 参数 + 优化器状态 + 每层的中间激活 × batch size。线性增长于层数 n。

2. **三种反传策略**（notebook markdown 部分）：
   - Vanilla backprop：保存全部中间结果，显存 O(n)，计算 O(n)
   - Low-memory backprop：什么都不存，每步重算，显存 O(1)（近似），计算 O(n²)
   - Gradient checkpointing：存 √n 个检查点，显存 O(√n)，计算 O(n√n)（额外一次前向）
   
3. **PyTorch 实现**：`torch.utils.checkpoint.checkpoint_sequential`
   - `self.classifier_modules = [module for k, module in self.classifier._modules.items()]`：把 Sequential 的子模块取出为列表
   - `x.requires_grad = True`：输入本来不需要梯度（是数据），checkpoint 机制要求至少一个输入 requires_grad=True 才能在反向时触发重算——这是著名的坑（如果所有输入都不需要梯度，反向传播时 checkpoint 内的梯度不会被计算/警告）
   - `checkpoint_sequential(functions=..., segments=1, input=x)`：把整个 classifier 作为 1 个 segment 包起来；前向不保存中间激活，反向时从 segment 边界重算
   
4. **segments 参数的权衡**：segments 越少越省显存但重算越多。notebook 作者选 segments=1。

5. **实测**：notebook 用 tracemalloc（Python 标准库，追踪 **CPU 内存**而非 GPU 显存！）。这是一个值得批判性阅读的点：tracemalloc 追踪的是 Python 分配器的内存，包括张量的 CPU 存储。严格说要测 GPU 显存应该用 `torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()`。实践任务正是要求用 torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated 实测 GPU 显存。notebook 用 tracemalloc 是一个便捷但间接的度量。我要指出这一点：实践任务用 torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats() + torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()。
   
   notebook 结论：峰值内存 143683 → 115055（约 -22%），训练时间 0.80 → 0.93 min（约 +14%）。两个版本训练损失完全一致（2.3045 → ... → 1.9474），说明检查点化不改变数学，只改变内存/时间权衡。

6. **受控对比方法论**：两次训练的超参、种子、数据完全一致，唯一差异是 forward 是否走 checkpoint_sequential。训练日志逐 batch 完全一致（因为 seed 相同且计算相同）。

7. **陷阱**：
   - `x.requires_grad = True` 的必要性：checkpoint 文档说至少一个输入需要 requires_grad，否则梯度不会流过重算段（此 notebook 因为输入是数据张量，默认 requires_grad=False，所以要显式设置）
   - ReLU(inplace=True) 与 checkpoint 的兼容性——本 notebook 用了 inplace=True 且能工作（torch 1.7）；重算时 inplace 操作可能有风险，但这里因为整体作为单个 segment 重算整个 forward，中间没有外部引用，所以安全。
   - Dropout / BatchNorm 这类依赖训练模式或有随机性的层：重算时随机数会重新采样，Dropout 两次前向掩码不同会导致梯度不精确！这是 checkpoint 的经典注意点：重算的前向必须与第一次前向产生相同的结果。PyTorch 通过保存 RNG 状态（use_reentrant 老版本的问题；torch.utils.checkpoint 默认会 fork RNG state 来保持 dropout 一致——实际上 checkpoint 有 preserve_rng_state=True 默认参数）。notebook 是 torch 1.7。这里我要小心陈述：新版 PyTorch 的 checkpoint 默认 preserve_rng_state=True，重算时恢复 RNG 状态，保证 Dropout 掩码一致。这个可以作为知识点提及，但注明版本差异，别过度断言 1.7 的行为。谨慎写法：「PyTorch 的 checkpoint 实现会在重算时恢复随机数状态（preserve_rng_state 默认为 True），以保证 Dropout 等随机层两次前向一致；老版本实现（use_reentrant 路径）与文档对这一点的描述随版本演进，使用时建议核对你所用版本的文档」。这样安全。
   - model.eval() 下 forward 也会走 checkpoint；推理不需要梯度，最好绕过 checkpoint（本 notebook 不区分，evaluate 时也会走 checkpoint_sequential，但由于 eval 时在 no_grad 下，checkpoint 前向不建图，只是多一次封装，没有重算开销——实际上 no_grad 下 checkpoint 直接前向，无额外重算）。
   - `model.cpu(); del model`：释放前一个模型的显存/内存，避免第二个实验被第一个模型污染——对比实验的内存隔离意识。

8. 数学部分：
   - Vanilla：显存 ∝ n（所有中间激活保存），每层计算 1 次前向
   - Low-memory：只存输入，每个节点需要时从头重算，计算 O(n²)
   - Checkpointing：√n 个检查点，显存 O(√n)，计算 O(n) 前向 + 每段重算 ≈ O(n) 额外前向，即约 2× 前向计算 + O(√n)·(段内重算)。精确的说法（Chen et al. 2016, Training Deep Nets with Sublinear Memory Cost）：显存 O(√n)，额外计算约一次前向。
   
   notebook markdown 的表述：「memory requirement increases by √n compared to the low-memory version」——注意 notebook 说的是相对于 low-memory 版本增加 √n。vanilla 处理 n 个节点，low-memory 处理 n² 个节点，checkpointing 介于其间。

9. NiN 结构回顾（承接 u3-l3）：三个 mlpconv 块（卷积 5×5/1×1/1×1）+ 两个池化 + 末尾 AvgPool2d(8) 全局平均池化输出 10 通道。参数量小、无全连接头。19 层的 Sequential（数一下：8+8+8 = 24 个模块：conv relu conv relu conv relu pool dropout ×2 + conv relu conv relu conv relu avgpool = 每块 8 个模块，第三块末尾 AvgPool。总 8+8+8=24 个子模块）。checkpoint_sequential 把 24 个模块按 segments 分组。

10. 实践任务设计（对应 manifest）：对 NiN 部分层应用 checkpoint，实测开关前后显存（torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated）与单 epoch 耗时，填「显存 vs 时间」对照表。具体步骤：
    - GPU 环境：torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats() 前重置，训练后 torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()/1024² 读 MB
    - 时间：time.perf_counter() 或训练日志的 Time elapsed
    - 对照组：baseline / 全模型 1 segment / segments=4 / segments=8
    - 无 GPU 的读者：用 tracemalloc 复现 notebook 原始对比 + 观察训练时间
    
11. 小练习：
    - 练习1：为什么 baseline 与 checkpoint 版第一个 batch 的 loss 完全一致（2.3045）？答案：相同 seed 下初始化与数据顺序相同，checkpoint 不改变前向计算的数学，只改变中间结果的保存策略。
    - 练习2：如果把 segments 从 1 改成 24（每层一段），会发生什么？答案：每个 segment 边界的输出都被保存，内存接近 vanilla（省不了多少），但重算开销也最小；segments=1 时只保存输入，最省显存但反向需重算整段前向。
    - 练习3：为什么 forward 里要写 x.requires_grad = True？答案：输入图像张量默认 requires_grad=False；checkpoint 的机制依赖「至少一个输入带梯度」来在反向时触发重算建图，若所有输入都不需要梯度，重算子图将得不到梯度。
    - 练习（关于 tracemalloc vs cuda）：tracemalloc 测的是什么内存？为什么实践任务推荐用 torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated？答案：tracemalloc 追踪 Python 堆（CPU 侧）分配；GPU 显存由 CUDA 分配器管理，tracemalloc 看不到，须用 torch.cuda 的统计 API。

def train_classifier_simple_v1(num_epochs, model, optimizer, device, 
                               train_loader, valid_loader=None, 
                               loss_fn=None, logging_interval=100, 
                               skip_epoch_stats=False):
    
    log_dict = {'train_loss_per_batch': [],
                'train_acc_per_epoch': [],
                'train_loss_per_epoch': [],
                'valid_acc_per_epoch': [],
                'valid_loss_per_epoch': []}
    
    if loss_fn is None:
        loss_fn = F.cross_entropy

    start_time = time.time()
    for epoch in range(num_epochs):

        model.train()
        for batch_idx, (features, targets) in enumerate(train_loader):

            features = features.to(device)
            targets = targets.to(device)

            # FORWARD AND BACK PROP
            logits = model(features)
            if isinstance(logits, torch.distributed.rpc.api.RRef):
                logits = logits.local_value()
            loss = loss_fn(logits, targets)
            optimizer.zero_grad()

            loss.backward()

            # UPDATE MODEL PARAMETERS
            optimizer.step()

            # LOGGING
            log_dict['train_loss_per_batch'].append(loss.item())

            if not batch_idx % logging_interval:
                print('Epoch: %03d/%03d | Batch %04d/%04d | Loss: %.4f'
                      % (epoch+1, num_epochs, batch_idx,
                          len(train_loader), loss))

        if not skip_epoch_stats:
            model.eval()

## 4.1 检查点原理
### 概念说明
两种极端 + 折中。checkpoint 的定义：前向时只保存少数「检查点」处的激活，其余在反向时按需重算。

### 核心流程
表格对比 + 伪代码：

vanilla:
```
for layer in layers: a[i] = layer(a[i-1])   # 全部 a[i] 存着
backward: 从 a[n] 往回，直接用保存的 a[i]
```

low-memory:
```
forward: 只存 a[0]
backward 第 i 层: 从 a[0] 重新前向算到 a[i-1]（重算！）
```

checkpointing:
```
forward: 存 a[0], a[√n], a[2√n], ...
backward: 在每个检查点段内重算段内前向
```

数学：
- vanilla 显存 O(n)、计算 O(n)
- low-memory 显存 O(1)（只存输入 + 边界）、计算 O(n²)
- checkpointing（每 √n 层设一个检查点）显存 O(√n)、额外计算约一次前向 O(n)

# 显存优化：梯度检查点

## 1. 本讲目标

学完本讲，你应该能够：

1. 说清楚训练时 GPU 显存都被什么占用，以及为什么「中间激活」是随网络深度和 batch size 线性膨胀的大头。
2. 解释梯度检查点（gradient checkpointing）的核心思想——**用重计算换显存**，以及它在「标准反向传播」与「低内存反向传播」两个极端之间如何折中出 \( O(\sqrt{n}) \) 的显存复杂度。
3. 会用 `torch.utils.checkpoint.checkpoint_sequential` 包装 `nn.Sequential` 模型，理解仓库 notebook 中三处 `###### NEW` 修改各自的用意（尤其是 `x.requires_grad = True` 这个著名的坑）。
4. 会实测「显存峰值 vs 训练时间」：GPU 上用 `torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()`，并批判性地理解仓库 notebook 用 `tracemalloc` 得到的数字到底测的是什么。
5. 建立「不改变数学、只改变内存策略」的受控对比意识：checkpoint 化前后逐 batch 损失应当完全一致。

本讲是第 8 单元「工程化与高级专题」的一讲，聚焦单卡显存不够时的**软件解法**（下一讲 u8-l5 的多 GPU 并行则是**硬件扩展解法**）。

## 2. 前置知识

### 2.1 训练时的显存账本

一次训练中，GPU 显存大致由四部分构成：

| 组成 | 大小 | 随什么增长 |
|---|---|---|
| 模型参数 | 每参数 4 字节（float32） | 与层数成正比 |
| 梯度 | 与参数同尺寸 | 与层数成正比 |
| 优化器状态 | Adam 额外存两份动量，约 2×参数量 | 与层数成正比 |
| **中间激活** | 每层的输入/输出特征图 | 与**层数 × batch size × 特征图尺寸**成正比 |

前三项只与参数量有关，对固定模型是常数；第四项「中间激活」才是真正的变量——batch size 翻倍、网络加深，它就翻倍。**梯度检查点针对的正是第四项。**

### 2.2 为什么中间激活必须保存

回顾 u2-l5 从零实现反向传播：第 \( l \) 层的权重梯度需要「上游误差项 × 本层输入」，即 \( \nabla_{W^{(l)}} = \delta^{(l)\top} a^{(l-1)} \)。PyTorch autograd 正是为此在前向时把每层的输入激活存进计算图，`loss.backward()` 时直接取用。也就是说：**标准 autograd 的「自动」是以把中间结果全留在显存里为代价的。**

### 2.3 本讲的主角模型：NiN

本讲沿用仓库 notebook 的载体——Network-in-Network（NiN）。u3-l3 已详细讲过它的设计哲学（1×1 卷积做跨通道升降维、末层输出类别数通道 + 全局平均池化、无全连接分类头），本讲只需记住它在这里的**结构角色**：一个由 23 个子模块顺序堆叠而成的 `nn.Sequential`，正好适合 `checkpoint_sequential` 这种「按序切段」的 API。作者在 notebook 中也说明了选择它的理由：结构简单、可读性好；网络越深，检查点的收益越大。

## 4. 核心概念与源码讲解

### 4.1 检查点原理：重计算换显存

#### 4.1.1 概念说明

设网络有 \( n \) 层。反向传播需要每层的中间激活，问题是：**这些激活什么时候存、存多少？** 两个极端：

- **标准反向传播（vanilla）**：前向时把所有中间激活都存下来。显存最省心，但显存开销 \( O(n) \)。
- **低内存反向传播（low-memory）**：前向什么都不存（只留输入），反向传到第 \( i \) 层时从输入**重新前向算到第 \( i \) 层**。显存几乎不随深度增长，但计算量变成 \( O(n^2) \)。

**梯度检查点是两者的折中**：只把少数层的激活定为「检查点」保存，其余激活反向时从最近的检查点**重算**出来。最优策略是每隔 \( \sqrt{n} \) 层设一个检查点，得到显存 \( O(\sqrt{n}) \)、额外计算约多一次前向的开销。这一思路的经典出处是 Chen et al. 2016《Training Deep Nets with Sublinear Memory Cost》（仓库 notebook 未直接引用该论文，但引用了四篇博客/教程，见下文源码精读）。

一句话直觉：**激活是可以「按需再生产」的商品——检查点就是仓库网点，网点越密，库存（显存）越高、运费（重算）越低；网点越疏，库存越省、运费越高。**

#### 4.1.2 核心流程

三种策略的伪代码对比（示例代码，用于理解而非仓库原文）：

```text
vanilla（标准 autograd）:
    前向: for i in 1..n: a[i] = layer_i(a[i-1])   # 所有 a[i] 留在显存
    反向: 逐层用现成的 a[i] 求梯度                  # 计算一遍

low-memory:
    前向: 只保留 a[0]（网络输入）
    反向: 求第 i 层梯度前，从 a[0] 一路重算到 a[i-1] # 每层都要重算 → O(n²)

gradient checkpointing（每 √n 层设检查点）:
    前向: 保存 a[0], a[√n], a[2√n], ...             # 只存 √n 份
    反向: 在每个检查点段内，从检查点激活重算段内前向   # 每段最多重算 √n 层
```

三者的权衡可以写成一张表（\( n \) 为层数）：

| 策略 | 中间激活显存 | 前向计算量 | 何时重算 |
|---|---|---|---|
| vanilla | \( O(n) \) | 1 次前向 | 从不 |
| low-memory | \( O(1) \) | \( O(n^2) \) | 每层都从头算 |
| checkpointing | \( O(\sqrt{n}) \) | 1 次前向 + 反向时各段重算（合计约多 1 次前向） | 每段从检查点重算 |

\[ \text{checkpointing 显存} = \underbrace{\sqrt{n}\ \text{份检查点激活}}_{O(\sqrt{n})} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \text{额外计算} \approx \text{一次完整前向} \]

注意 notebook 原文的表述角度略有不同：它说 checkpointing 的内存需求「比 low-memory 版本增加 \( \sqrt{n} \）」，且处理节点数介于 vanilla 的 \( n \) 与 low-memory 的 \( n^2 \) 之间——同一结论的另两种说法。

仓库 notebook 开头的理论说明 cell 完整讲述了上述三种策略：

#### 4.1.5 小练习与答案

**练习 1**：为什么说梯度检查点「不改变训练的数学，只改变内存策略」？

**答案**：重算得到的是同一组中间激活（相同权重、相同输入下前向是确定性的），因此各层梯度与标准反传完全一致，最终参数更新也一致。它只是把「保存」变成「需要时再算」，改变的是显存与时间的分配，不是计算结果。（本讲 4.3.3 会看到两个版本逐 batch 损失完全一致的实证。）

**练习 2**：如果你的模型只有 2 层，用梯度检查点划算吗？

**答案**：不划算。\( \sqrt{2} \approx 1.4 \)，能省下的激活寥寥无几，而反向时的重算开销是实打实的。检查点的收益随深度增长，所以 notebook 作者也说「架构越深，收益越大」；对极浅模型应优先考虑减小 batch size 或改用混合精度。

**练习 3**：检查点数量（`segments` 语义见 4.2）取两个极端——「每层都是检查点」和「全网只有 1 个检查点」——分别退化成 4.1.2 表中的哪种策略？

**答案**：每层都是检查点 ⇒ 反向时几乎不需要重算、但全部激活都保存 ⇒ 退化成 vanilla；全网 1 个检查点（只保存网络输入）⇒ 反向时要重算整个前向 ⇒ 显存最省、重算最多，接近 low-memory（但重算只发生在反向一次，仍是 \( O(n) \) 而非 \( O(n^2) \)）。仓库 notebook 选择的 `segments=1` 正是后者的温和版。

### 4.2 `torch.utils.checkpoint` 的使用

#### 4.2.1 概念说明

PyTorch 把检查点机制做进了标准库：`torch.utils.checkpoint` 模块提供两个入口——

- `checkpoint(function, *args)`：把**任意一段可微计算**包成一个检查点段；
- `checkpoint_sequential(functions, segments, input)`：**顺序模型专用**，把一个模块列表切成 `segments` 段，段边界即检查点。

从外部看，`checkpoint_sequential` 的输入输出与直接调用原模型没有任何区别（forward 的返回值一模一样），因此 notebook 中**训练循环、损失函数、优化器一行都不用改**——这正是它「即插即用」的工程价值。变化全部发生在 autograd 内部：

- **前向**：段内以不建图的方式（`no_grad` 语义）执行，中间激活用完即弃，只保存每个段的**输入**；
- **反向**：autograd 走到某个段时，从该段的输入**重算**段内前向、这次建图，然后在图内正常反传。

`segments` 是显存-时间旋钮：段数越少越省显存、重算越多；段数越多越接近 vanilla。仓库作者的取舍写在 Part 2 的说明里——对该 NiN 而言 `segments=1` 已经是好的折中。

#### 4.2.2 核心流程

把 23 个模块的 NiN 接入检查点后的单步训练流程：

```text
1. x (B,3,32,32) 进入 forward
2. x.requires_grad = True          # 让"段输入"参与梯度图（关键，见下）
3. checkpoint_sequential(modules, segments=1, x)
   ├─ 前向（不建图）: 逐模块算到 AvgPool2d(8)，输出 (B,10,1,1)，中间激活即弃
   └─ autograd 登记"重算闭包"：(段输入 x, 段内模块列表)
4. view 成 (B,10) 得 logits → cross_entropy → loss
5. loss.backward()
   └─ 走到检查点段: 用保存的 x 重算段内前向（这次建图）→ 正常反传得到所有参数梯度
6. optimizer.step()                # 与不检查点化完全相同的更新
```

**`x.requires_grad = True` 为什么必须？** 输入图像是数据张量，`requires_grad` 默认为 `False`；而被检查点包裹的段要求「至少一个输入带梯度」，反向传播才会为该段触发重算建图——否则段内参数会拿不到梯度。这是 `torch.utils.checkpoint` 文档明示的经典陷阱，notebook 用一行赋值解决。（较新版本的 PyTorch 提供了非重入实现 `use_reentrant=False`，对这一要求有所放宽；不同版本行为有差异，使用时请以你所用版本的官方文档为准。）

**Dropout 怎么办？** 重算的前向必须与第一次前向产生**相同**的结果，否则梯度就不精确。NiN 里有两个 `Dropout(0.5)`——两次前向若采样出不同的掩码，重算就不再等价。PyTorch 的 `checkpoint` 默认会在前向时保存随机数状态、重算时恢复（`preserve_rng_state=True`），以保证 Dropout 这类随机层前后一致。这一行为是默认保证而非巧合，但仍建议你在自己版本上核对文档。

**练习 1**：`checkpoint_sequential(functions=..., segments=..., input=...)` 中的 `segments=1` 是什么含义？保存了什么、丢掉了什么？

**答案**：`segments=1` 表示把整个模块列表切成 1 段——只保存该段的输入（即网络输入 x）与输出，其余 22 个模块间激活全部不保存；反向传播时从 x 重算整条前向（这次建图）再反传。显存最省，重算等于多跑一次完整前向。

**练习 2**：如果删掉 `x.requires_grad = True` 这一行，会发生什么？

**答案**：被包裹段的全部输入（只有 x）都不带梯度标志，反向传播不会为该段触发重算建图，段内所有卷积核**拿不到梯度**（PyTorch 还会给出警告），训练实际上失效。这是官方文档明示的使用前提，notebook 用这一行显式满足它。

**练习 3**：为什么重算时 Dropout 的掩码必须与第一次前向一致？PyTorch 如何保证？

**答案**：若两次前向的 Dropout 掩码不同，「重算出的激活」与「损失所依据的激活」就不是同一个函数的输出，梯度方向就是错的。PyTorch 的 `checkpoint` 默认在前向时保存 RNG 状态、重算前恢复（`preserve_rng_state=True`），使第二次采样与第一次完全一致。

### 4.3 显存与时间实测

#### 4.3.1 概念说明

「显存优化了多少」必须实测。两条路线：

- **`tracemalloc`（Python 标准库）**：追踪 **Python 解释器堆**上的内存分配（`tracemalloc.start()` 开始追踪，`get_traced_memory()` 返回 `(当前, 峰值)`，单位字节）。它是**CPU 侧**的度量——**看不到 CUDA 显存**（GPU 张量由 CUDA 分配器管理，不经过 Python 堆）。
- **`torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()`**：PyTorch CUDA 缓存分配器的统计口径，返回自上次 `torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()` 以来**实际分配的 GPU 显存峰值**——这才是「显存够不够」的直接证据。

仓库 notebook 用的是 `tracemalloc`。这带来了一个值得批判性阅读的点：notebook 的训练明明跑在 GPU 上（`Device: cuda:2`），但 143,683 字节（约 140 KiB）这个峰值显然**不是** GPU 显存占用（光模型参数与梯度就远超此数）——它测到的是 Python 侧对象（如 autograd 图的簿记等）的堆内存差异。作为「检查点减少了需要簿记的中间对象」的**间接证据**它是有效的，但严格意义上的 GPU 显存收益应当用 `torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()` 直接测量——这正是本讲实践任务要补上的实验。

同理，时间维度的度量要用 `time.perf_counter()`（或训练日志里的 `Time elapsed` / `Total Training Time`），并注意首次运行包含 CUDA 预热，正式计时前最好先跑几个 batch 热身。

#### 4.3.2 核心流程

一次规范的「显存 vs 时间」实测流程：

```text
1. 实验隔离: model.cpu(); del model; torch.cuda.empty_cache()   # 清掉上一个实验
2. 重建: set_all_seeds(seed) → 模型 → optimizer                  # 与基线完全同参
3. 计时器清零: start = time.perf_counter()
   显存统计清零: torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
4. 训练固定 epoch 数（训练循环与基线完全相同）
5. 读数: elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
        peak   = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 1024**2      # MB
6. 填表对比，计算相对变化时先声明以谁为基准
```

#### 4.3.5 小练习与答案

**练习 1**：为什么 `tracemalloc` 的读数（约 140 KB）不能当作该实验的真实显存占用？

**答案**：`tracemalloc` 追踪的是 Python 解释器堆的分配；GPU 张量的存储由 PyTorch 的 CUDA 缓存分配器经 CUDA API 管理，不经过 Python 堆，因此对 `tracemalloc` 不可见。140 KB 只反映 Python 侧对象（如 autograd 簿记）的差异。GPU 显存要用 `torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()` 度量。

**练习 2**：为什么实测脚本里在正式计时前要做「热身」并调用 `torch.cuda.synchronize()`？

**答案**：首次执行会触发 cuDNN 卷积算法选择、CUDA 上下文与 kernel 编译等一次性开销，直接计入会高估耗时；CUDA 调用是异步的，`perf_counter` 取读数前必须 `synchronize()` 确保此前提交的 GPU 工作全部完成，否则测到的是「提交时间」而非「执行时间」。

**练习 3**：`max_memory_allocated` 与 `memory_allocated` 有何区别？为什么对比实验更应关注前者？

**答案**：`memory_allocated` 是**当前**时刻已分配的显存，`max_memory_allocated` 是自峰值计数器重置以来的**历史最高值**。反向传播阶段（激活 + 梯度 + 优化器状态叠加）往往才是显存峰值，用瞬时值会系统性低估「是否 OOM」的风险，因此 OOM 分析与省显存对比都应看峰值。

## 5. 综合实践

**任务：用梯度检查点「救活」一个 OOM 的训练配置，并量化代价。**

把本讲所有内容串成一次完整实验（建议在 GPU 环境进行）：

1. **制造显存压力**：以 notebook 的检查点版 NiN 为基础，逐步调大 `BATCH_SIZE`（256 → 512 → 1024 …），只训基线版（无检查点），找到**第一个**触发 `CUDA out of memory` 的 batch size，记为 \( B_{\text{oom}} \)。这一步验证 2.1 的账本：显存压力主要来自「中间激活 × batch size」。
2. **检查点救援**：对同一个 \( B_{\text{oom}} \)（可先试 \( B_{\text{oom}} \) 与其一半），切换到 `segments=1` 的检查点版重新训练——预期能跑通；若仍 OOM，把模型中两个池化后的子列表再各包一层 `checkpoint_sequential`（改 `segments` 或分组包装）。
3. **量化代价**：用 4.3.4 的 `run_benchmark` 流程，对「基线 + 可行的最大 batch」「检查点 + 同 batch」「检查点 + \( B_{\text{oom}} \)」三组配置测量单 epoch 耗时与显存峰值。
4. **产出一张实验报告表**，至少包含：配置、batch size、是否 OOM、显存峰值 (MB)、单 epoch 耗时 (s)、2 epoch 后训练准确率，以及一段结论：**你的环境下检查点把可行的 batch size 上限推高了多少？时间代价是多少？**

预期：检查点版在相同 batch size 下显存显著下降、耗时上升；在 \( B_{\text{oom}} \) 下「跑得慢总比跑不了强」——这正是仓库 notebook 开头说的场景：「当 GPU 显存是硬限制、连减小 batch size 都无法绕开时，梯度检查点是让一切跑起来的简单选项」。具体数字**待本地验证**。

## 6. 本讲小结

- 训练显存的变量大头是**中间激活**（随层数 × batch size 线性增长）；标准 autograd 之所以「自动」，是因为它把所有中间激活留在显存里备用。
- 梯度检查点在「全保存（vanilla，显存 \( O(n) \)）」与「全重算（low-memory，计算 \( O(n^2) \)）」之间折中：每 \( \sqrt{n} \) 层存一个检查点，显存 \( O(\sqrt{n}) \)，代价约多一次前向——**用重计算换显存**。
- 仓库 notebook 的接入方式只有三处修改：导入 `checkpoint_sequential`、把 `Sequential._modules` 取成模块列表、`forward` 里 `x.requires_grad = True` 后调用 `checkpoint_sequential(functions=..., segments=1, input=x)`；训练循环零改动。
- `x.requires_grad = True` 是关键坑：段的所有输入都不带梯度时，反向不会为该段重算建图，参数拿不到梯度；Dropout 的一致性由 checkpoint 默认保存/恢复 RNG 状态保证。
- 两个版本逐 batch 损失**完全一致**（2.3045 → … → 1.9474），实证检查点不改变训练数学；实验卫生上，两次运行之间要 `model.cpu(); del model` 隔离内存。
- notebook 用 `tracemalloc` 测得峰值 143,683 → 115,055 字节（作者结论约 −22%）、耗时 0.80 → 0.93 min（约 +14%）；注意 `tracemalloc` 是 Python 堆口径、看不到 CUDA 显存，严格的显存实测应使用 `torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()` + `torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()`。

## 7. 下一步学习建议

- **下一讲 u8-l5（多 GPU 并行）**：当单卡显存与算力都不够时，`DataParallel` 把 batch 拆分到多卡、流水线并行把模型按层切分——与本讲的「单卡省显存」互补，两者可以叠加使用。

# 显存优化：梯度检查点

## 1. 本讲目标

学完本讲，你应该能够：

1. 说清楚训练时 GPU 显存都被什么占用，以及为什么「中间激活」是随网络深度和 batch size 线性膨胀的大头。
2. 解释梯度检查点（gradient checkpointing）的核心思想——**用重计算换显存**，以及它在「标准反向传播」与「低内存反向传播」两个极端之间如何折中出 \( O(\sqrt{n}) \) 的显存复杂度。
3. 会用 `torch.utils.checkpoint.checkpoint_sequential` 包装 `nn.Sequential` 模型，理解仓库 notebook 中三处 `###### NEW` 修改各自的用意（尤其是 `x.requires_grad = True` 这个著名的坑）。
4. 会实测「显存峰值 vs 训练时间」：GPU 上用 `torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()`，并批判性地理解仓库 notebook 用 `tracemalloc` 得到的数字到底测的是什么。
5. 建立「不改变数学、只改变内存策略」的受控对比意识：checkpoint 化前后逐 batch 损失应当完全一致。

本讲是第 8 单元「工程化与高级专题」的一讲，聚焦单卡显存不够时的**软件解法**（下一讲 u8-l5 的多 GPU 并行则是**硬件扩展解法**）。

## 2. 前置知识

### 2.1 训练时的显存账本

一次训练中，GPU 显存大致由四部分构成：

| 组成 | 大小 | 随什么增长 |
|---|---|---|
| 模型参数 | 每参数 4 字节（float32） | 与层数成正比 |
| 梯度 | 与参数同尺寸 | 与层数成正比 |
| 优化器状态 | Adam 额外存两份动量，约 2×参数量 | 与层数成正比 |
| **中间激活** | 每层的输入/输出特征图 | 与**层数 × batch size × 特征图尺寸**成正比 |

前三项只与参数量有关，对固定模型是常数；第四项「中间激活」才是真正的变量——batch size 翻倍、网络加深，它就翻倍。**梯度检查点针对的正是第四项。**

### 2.2 为什么中间激活必须保存

回顾 u2-l5 从零实现反向传播：第 \( l \) 层的权重梯度需要「上游误差项 × 本层输入」，即 \( \nabla_{W^{(l)}} = \delta^{(l)\top} a^{(l-1)} \)。PyTorch autograd 正是为此在前向时把每层的输入激活存进计算图，`loss.backward()` 时直接取用。也就是说：**标准 autograd 的「自动」是以把中间结果全留在显存里为代价的。**

### 2.3 本讲的主角模型：NiN

本讲沿用仓库 notebook 的载体——Network-in-Network（NiN）。u3-l3 已详细讲过它的设计哲学（1×1 卷积做跨通道升降维、末层输出类别数通道 + 全局平均池化、无全连接分类头），本讲只需记住它在这里的**结构角色**：一个由 23 个子模块顺序堆叠而成的 `nn.Sequential`，正好适合 `checkpoint_sequential` 这种「按序切段」的 API。作者在 notebook 中也说明了选择它的理由：结构简单、可读性好；网络越深，检查点的收益越大。

## 4. 核心概念与源码讲解

### 4.1 检查点原理：重计算换显存

#### 4.1.1 概念说明

设网络有 \( n \) 层。反向传播需要每层的中间激活，问题是：**这些激活什么时候存、存多少？** 两个极端：

- **标准反向传播（vanilla）**：前向时把所有中间激活都存下来。显存最省心，但显存开销 \( O(n) \)。
- **低内存反向传播（low-memory）**：前向什么都不存（只留输入），反向传到第 \( i \) 层时从输入**重新前向算到第 \( i \) 层**。显存几乎不随深度增长，但计算量变成 \( O(n^2) \)。

**梯度检查点是两者的折中**：只把少数层的激活定为「检查点」保存，其余激活反向时从最近的检查点**重算**出来。最优策略是每隔 \( \sqrt{n} \) 层设一个检查点，得到显存 \( O(\sqrt{n}) \)、额外计算约多一次前向的开销。这一思路的经典出处是 Chen et al. 2016《Training Deep Nets with Sublinear Memory Cost》（仓库 notebook 未直接引用该论文，但引用了四篇博客/教程，见下文源码精读）。

一句话直觉：**激活是可以「按需再生产」的商品——检查点就是仓库网点，网点越密，库存（显存）越高、运费（重算）越低；网点越疏，库存越省、运费越高。**

#### 4.1.2 核心流程

三种策略的伪代码对比（示例代码，用于理解而非仓库原文）：

```text
vanilla（标准 autograd）:
    前向: for i in 1..n: a[i] = layer_i(a[i-1])   # 所有 a[i] 留在显存
    反向: 逐层用现成的 a[i] 求梯度                  # 计算一遍

low-memory:
    前向: 只保留 a[0]（网络输入）
    反向: 求第 i 层梯度前，从 a[0] 一路重算到 a[i-1] # 每层都要重算 → O(n²)

gradient checkpointing（每 √n 层设检查点）:
    前向: 保存 a[0], a[√n], a[2√n], ...             # 只存 √n 份
    反向: 在每个检查点段内，从检查点激活重算段内前向   # 每段最多重算 √n 层
```

三者的权衡可以写成一张表（\( n \) 为层数）：

| 策略 | 中间激活显存 | 前向计算量 | 何时重算 |
|---|---|---|---|
| vanilla | \( O(n) \) | 1 次前向 | 从不 |
| low-memory | \( O(1) \) | \( O(n^2) \) | 每层都从头算 |
| checkpointing | \( O(\sqrt{n}) \) | 1 次前向 + 反向时各段重算（合计约多 1 次前向） | 每段从检查点重算 |

\[ \text{checkpointing 显存} = \underbrace{\sqrt{n}\ \text{份检查点激活}}_{O(\sqrt{n})} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \text{额外计算} \approx \text{一次完整前向} \]

注意 notebook 原文的表述角度略有不同：它说 checkpointing 的内存需求「比 low-memory 版本增加 \( \sqrt{n} \）」，且处理节点数介于 vanilla 的 \( n \) 与 low-memory 的 \( n^2 \) 之间——同一结论的另两种说法。

仓库 notebook 开头的理论说明 cell 完整讲述了上述三种策略：

#### 4.1.5 小练习与答案

**练习 1**：为什么说梯度检查点「不改变训练的数学，只改变内存策略」？

**答案**：重算得到的是同一组中间激活（相同权重、相同输入下前向是确定性的），因此各层梯度与标准反传完全一致，最终参数更新也一致。它只是把「保存」变成「需要时再算」，改变的是显存与时间的分配，不是计算结果。（本讲 4.3.3 会看到两个版本逐 batch 损失完全一致的实证。）

**练习 2**：如果你的模型只有 2 层，用梯度检查点划算吗？

**答案**：不划算。\( \sqrt{2} \approx 1.4 \)，能省下的激活寥寥无几，而反向时的重算开销是实打实的。检查点的收益随深度增长，所以 notebook 作者也说「架构越深，收益越大」；对极浅模型应优先考虑减小 batch size 或改用混合精度。

**练习 3**：检查点数量（`segments` 语义见 4.2）取两个极端——「每层都是检查点」和「全网只有 1 个检查点」——分别退化成 4.1.2 表中的哪种策略？

**答案**：每层都是检查点 ⇒ 反向时几乎不需要重算、但全部激活都保存 ⇒ 退化成 vanilla；全网 1 个检查点（只保存网络输入）⇒ 反向时要重算整个前向 ⇒ 显存最省、重算最多，接近 low-memory（但重算只发生在反向一次，仍是 \( O(n) \) 而非 \( O(n^2) \)）。仓库 notebook 选择的 `segments=1` 正是后者的温和版。

### 4.2 `torch.utils.checkpoint` 的使用

#### 4.2.1 概念说明

PyTorch 把检查点机制做进了标准库：`torch.utils.checkpoint` 模块提供两个入口——

- `checkpoint(function, *args)`：把**任意一段可微计算**包成一个检查点段；
- `checkpoint_sequential(functions, segments, input)`：**顺序模型专用**，把一个模块列表切成 `segments` 段，段边界即检查点。

从外部看，`checkpoint_sequential` 的输入输出与直接调用原模型没有任何区别（forward 的返回值一模一样），因此 notebook 中**训练循环、损失函数、优化器一行都不用改**——这正是它「即插即用」的工程价值。变化全部发生在 autograd 内部：

- **前向**：段内以不建图的方式（`no_grad` 语义）执行，中间激活用完即弃，只保存每个段的**输入**；
- **反向**：autograd 走到某个段时，从该段的输入**重算**段内前向、这次建图，然后在图内正常反传。

`segments` 是显存-时间旋钮：段数越少越省显存、重算越多；段数越多越接近 vanilla。仓库作者的取舍写在 Part 2 的说明里——对该 NiN 而言 `segments=1` 已经是好的折中。

#### 4.2.2 核心流程

把 23 个模块的 NiN 接入检查点后的单步训练流程：

```text
1. x (B,3,32,32) 进入 forward
2. x.requires_grad = True          # 让"段输入"参与梯度图（关键，见下）
3. checkpoint_sequential(modules, segments=1, x)
   ├─ 前向（不建图）: 逐模块算到 AvgPool2d(8)，输出 (B,10,1,1)，中间激活即弃
   └─ autograd 登记"重算闭包"：(段输入 x, 段内模块列表)
4. view 成 (B,10) 得 logits → cross_entropy → loss
5. loss.backward()
   └─ 走到检查点段: 用保存的 x 重算段内前向（这次建图）→ 正常反传得到所有参数梯度
6. optimizer.step()                # 与不检查点化完全相同的更新
```

**`x.requires_grad = True` 为什么必须？** 输入图像是数据张量，`requires_grad` 默认为 `False`；而被检查点包裹的段要求「至少一个输入带梯度」，反向传播才会为该段触发重算建图——否则段内参数会拿不到梯度。这是 `torch.utils.checkpoint` 文档明示的经典陷阱，notebook 用一行赋值解决。（较新版本的 PyTorch 提供了非重入实现 `use_reentrant=False`，对这一要求有所放宽；不同版本行为有差异，使用时请以你所用版本的官方文档为准。）

**Dropout 怎么办？** 重算的前向必须与第一次前向产生**相同**的结果，否则梯度就不精确。NiN 里有两个 `Dropout(0.5)`——两次前向若采样出不同的掩码，重算就不再等价。PyTorch 的 `checkpoint` 默认会在前向时保存随机数状态、重算时恢复（`preserve_rng_state=True`），以保证 Dropout 这类随机层前后一致。这一行为是默认保证而非巧合，但仍建议你在自己版本上核对文档。

**练习 1**：`checkpoint_sequential(functions=..., segments=..., input=...)` 中的 `segments=1` 是什么含义？保存了什么、丢掉了什么？

**答案**：`segments=1` 表示把整个模块列表切成 1 段——只保存该段的输入（即网络输入 x）与输出，其余 22 个模块间激活全部不保存；反向传播时从 x 重算整条前向（这次建图）再反传。显存最省，重算等于多跑一次完整前向。

**练习 2**：如果删掉 `x.requires_grad = True` 这一行，会发生什么？

**答案**：被包裹段的全部输入（只有 x）都不带梯度标志，反向传播不会为该段触发重算建图，段内所有卷积核**拿不到梯度**（PyTorch 还会给出警告），训练实际上失效。这是官方文档明示的使用前提，notebook 用这一行显式满足它。

**练习 3**：为什么重算时 Dropout 的掩码必须与第一次前向一致？PyTorch 如何保证？

**答案**：若两次前向的 Dropout 掩码不同，「重算出的激活」与「损失所依据的激活」就不是同一个函数的输出，梯度方向就是错的。PyTorch 的 `checkpoint` 默认在前向时保存 RNG 状态、重算前恢复（`preserve_rng_state=True`），使第二次采样与第一次完全一致。

#### 4.3.1 概念说明

「显存优化了多少」必须实测。两条路线：

- **`tracemalloc`（Python 标准库）**：追踪 **Python 解释器堆**上的内存分配（`tracemalloc.start()` 开始追踪，`get_traced_memory()` 返回 `(当前, 峰值)`，单位字节）。它是**CPU 侧**的度量——**看不到 CUDA 显存**（GPU 张量由 CUDA 分配器管理，不经过 Python 堆）。
- **`torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()`**：PyTorch CUDA 缓存分配器的统计口径，返回自上次 `torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()` 以来**实际分配的 GPU 显存峰值**——这才是「显存够不够」的直接证据。

#### 4.3.2 核心流程

一次规范的「显存 vs 时间」实测流程：

```text
1. 实验隔离: model.cpu(); del model; torch.cuda.empty_cache()   # 清掉上一个实验
2. 重建: set_all_seeds(seed) → 模型 → optimizer                  # 与基线完全同参
3. 计时器清零: start = time.perf_counter()
   显存统计清零: torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
4. 训练固定 epoch 数（训练循环与基线完全相同）
5. 读数: elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
        peak   = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 1024**2      # MB
6. 填表对比，计算相对变化时先声明以谁为基准
```

#### 4.3.5 小练习与答案

**练习 1**：为什么 `tracemalloc` 的读数（约 140 KB）不能当作该实验的真实显存占用？

**答案**：`tracemalloc` 追踪的是 Python 解释器堆的分配；GPU 张量的存储由 PyTorch 的 CUDA 缓存分配器经 CUDA API 管理，不经过 Python 堆，因此对 `tracemalloc` 不可见。140 KB 只反映 Python 侧对象（如 autograd 簿记）的差异。GPU 显存要用 `torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()` 度量。

**练习 2**：为什么实测脚本里在正式计时前要做「热身」并调用 `torch.cuda.synchronize()`？

**答案**：首次执行会触发 cuDNN 卷积算法选择、CUDA 上下文与 kernel 编译等一次性开销，直接计入会高估耗时；CUDA 调用是异步的，`perf_counter` 取读数前必须 `synchronize()` 确保此前提交的 GPU 工作全部完成，否则测到的是「提交时间」而非「执行时间」。

**练习 3**：`max_memory_allocated` 与 `memory_allocated` 有何区别？为什么对比实验更应关注前者？

**答案**：`memory_allocated` 是**当前**时刻已分配的显存，`max_memory_allocated` 是自峰值计数器重置以来的**历史最高值**。反向传播阶段（激活 + 梯度 + 优化器状态叠加）往往才是显存峰值，用瞬时值会系统性低估「是否 OOM」的风险，因此 OOM 分析与省显存对比都应看峰值。

## 5. 综合实践

**任务：用梯度检查点「救活」一个 OOM 的训练配置，并量化代价。**

把本讲所有内容串成一次完整实验（建议在 GPU 环境进行）：

1. **制造显存压力**：以 notebook 的检查点版 NiN 为基础，逐步调大 `BATCH_SIZE`（256 → 512 → 1024 …），只训基线版（无检查点），找到**第一个**触发 `CUDA out of memory` 的 batch size，记为 \( B_{\text{oom}} \)。这一步验证 2.1 的账本：显存压力主要来自「中间激活 × batch size」。
2. **检查点救援**：对同一个 \( B_{\text{oom}} \)（可先试 \( B_{\text{oom}} \) 与其一半），切换到 `segments=1` 的检查点版重新训练——预期能跑通；若仍 OOM，把模型中两个池化后的子列表再各包一层 `checkpoint_sequential`（改 `segments` 或分组包装）。
3. **量化代价**：用 4.3.4 的 `run_benchmark` 流程，对「基线 + 可行的最大 batch」「检查点 + 同 batch」「检查点 + \( B_{\text{oom}} \)」三组配置测量单 epoch 耗时与显存峰值。
4. **产出一张实验报告表**，至少包含：配置、batch size、是否 OOM、显存峰值 (MB)、单 epoch 耗时 (s)、2 epoch 后训练准确率，以及一段结论：**你的环境下检查点把可行的 batch size 上限推高了多少？时间代价是多少？**

预期：检查点版在相同 batch size 下显存显著下降、耗时上升；在 \( B_{\text{oom}} \) 下「跑得慢总比跑不了强」——这正是仓库 notebook 开头说的场景：「当 GPU 显存是硬限制、连减小 batch size 都无法绕开时，梯度检查点是让一切跑起来的简单选项」。具体数字**待本地验证**。

## 6. 本讲小结

- 训练显存的变量大头是**中间激活**（随层数 × batch size 线性增长）；标准 autograd 之所以「自动」，是因为它把所有中间激活留在显存里备用。
- 梯度检查点在「全保存（vanilla，显存 \( O(n) \)）」与「全重算（low-memory，计算 \( O(n^2) \)）」之间折中：每 \( \sqrt{n} \) 层存一个检查点，显存 \( O(\sqrt{n}) \)，代价约多一次前向——**用重计算换显存**。
- 仓库 notebook 的接入方式只有三处修改：导入 `checkpoint_sequential`、把 `Sequential._modules` 取成模块列表、`forward` 里 `x.requires_grad = True` 后调用 `checkpoint_sequential(functions=..., segments=1, input=x)`；训练循环零改动。
- `x.requires_grad = True` 是关键坑：段的所有输入都不带梯度时，反向不会为该段重算建图，参数拿不到梯度；Dropout 的一致性由 checkpoint 默认保存/恢复 RNG 状态保证。

- notebook 用 `tracemalloc` 测得峰值 143,683 → 115,055 字节（作者结论约 −22%）、耗时 0.80 → 0.93 min（约 +14%）；注意 `tracemalloc` 是 Python 堆口径、看不到 CUDA 显存，严格的显存实测应使用 `torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()` + `torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()`。

## 7. 下一步学习建议

- **下一讲 u8-l5（多 GPU 并行）**：当单卡显存与算力都不够时，`DataParallel` 把 batch 拆分到多卡、流水线并行把模型按层切分——与本讲的「单卡省显存」互补，两者可以叠加使用。

- **回到代码**：把 4.3.4 的 benchmark 脚本套用到你自己在 u3/u5 学过的更深的模型上（如 ResNet-50、DenseNet-121），验证「越深收益越大」的说法；再对照仓库 [pytorch_ipynb/cnn/nin-cifar10.ipynb](https://github.com/rasbt/deeplearning-models/blob/59beda3aa25337e576564f1c18c6edd26f9f30e3/pytorch_ipynb/cnn/nin-cifar10.ipynb) 看 NiN 完整 40 epoch 训练版的用法。
